analysis.one_liner: Taxed coal, oil, and natural gas based on their carbon content to cut carbon dioxide emissions.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor in the two years it was pending.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a new federal excise tax on fossil fuels, charged at the point of sale or import: $18 per ton of coal, $3.90 per barrel of petroleum, and 48 cents per thousand cubic feet of natural gas, with rates phasing in over four years and rising with inflation afterward. The stated purpose was to reduce carbon dioxide emissions, the main driver of climate change. The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee, and no other member signed on.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially younger generations and communities vulnerable to air pollution and climate change, would benefit from reduced carbon dioxide emissions. Communities affected by coal mining and fossil fuel combustion would see less pollution. Over time, a rising carbon price pushes energy production toward cleaner sources.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone exposed to pollution and climate risk

how_it_helps.text: The bill states its purpose in its title: to reduce emissions of carbon dioxide by taxing coal, petroleum, and natural gas based on their carbon content [S3].

The tax applies to coal at $18 per ton, petroleum at $3.90 per barrel, and natural gas at 48 cents per thousand cubic feet, making dirtier fuels relatively more expensive than cleaner alternatives [S3].
Rates phase in gradually starting in 1992 at one-fifth of the full rate, giving producers and consumers time to adjust, and rise with inflation after 1992 so the incentive does not erode [S3].
The tax applies to imports of coal and natural gas and to exported fuels that were never taxed, so foreign fuel cannot undercut the policy [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, refiners, and importers owe the tax directly, but excise taxes are largely passed through to consumers in the form of higher prices for gasoline, electricity, and heating fuel. Households that use a lot of energy, including lower-income households, would feel this most, and the bill contains no rebate or offset to cushion them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Energy producers, and ultimately energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The bill only imposes the tax; it contains no provision returning the revenue to households, so the higher energy prices it creates would fall hardest on lower-income families who spend a larger share of income on fuel and electricity [S3].

A carbon tax raises costs for energy-intensive industries such as manufacturing and utilities, which can translate into higher prices for goods and job pressure in coal and oil-producing regions [S3].
A unilateral tax on domestic fuels and imports could put U.S. producers at a price disadvantage against foreign competitors in energy-intensive goods [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward carbon tax: it attacks emissions at the source with steadily rising rates, which is the design most economists favor, and its phase-in softens the shock. But it is also incomplete — an honest supporter would acknowledge that it raises energy prices for everyone without any rebate to offset the burden on lower-income households. Its main weakness as a bill was political, not technical: it drew no cosponsors and was never taken up.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark of California introduced the bill on February 21, 1991 [S1].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
That was the last action ever taken on the bill; the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup [S5].
No member of the House cosponsored the bill during the entire two-year Congress [S4].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and all bills not passed by then die automatically [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, petroleum, and natural gas producers are better off — no carbon tax was ever enacted, so their fuels faced no new levy. Households kept lower energy prices in the short run but did not get the emissions reductions the bill sought.

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its only sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over all tax legislation, chaired by Rep. Dan Rostenkowski (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: House members
against.what_they_did: No member signed on as a cosponsor at any point during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member cosponsored, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill taxes coal at $18 per ton, the steepest per-unit rate of the three fuels, reflecting coal's high carbon content. Industry revenue and demand would fall as the rate phased in.
A $3.90-per-barrel tax on all petroleum products including crude oil would raise costs across gasoline, diesel, and heating oil, passed through to consumers.

industries.industry: Natural gas producers and pipeline operators
industries.note: Pipeline operators would be responsible for paying the 48-cents-per-thousand-cubic-feet tax on gas received at U.S. pipeline facilities, including imports.

industries.industry: Coal-fired electric utilities and energy-intensive manufacturers
industries.note: These industries buy fossil fuels in bulk and would face higher input costs, which they would pass on in electricity rates and product prices.
